# Machine Learning {#sec-machine-learning}

The models in @sec-modeling include logistic and Poisson regression for 311
request outcomes. These are statistical models, and they are also examples
of supervised machine learning when the goal is to predict a known outcome
from features. Statistics and machine learning overlap; they differ more in
their emphases than in a clean boundary. Statistical modeling often
emphasizes a specified relationship, uncertainty, and interpretation.
Machine learning often emphasizes predictive performance and procedures
that learn patterns from data. Both fields develop methods for explanation
and prediction [@james2023introduction].

This chapter places the models from @sec-modeling in a broader map of
learning methods. It introduces common learning tasks, explains why
performance on new data matters, and shows how tuning and pipelines fit into
model development. The worked examples in @sec-modeling demonstrate model
fitting, score calculation, tuning, and prediction evaluation.


## Learning Settings

Learning methods differ partly in the feedback available during learning.
Let $X$ denote input features and, when an outcome is observed, let $Y$
denote that outcome. These symbols describe the information available to a
learning procedure; they do not determine which method is appropriate or
what conclusions its results support.


| Setting | Feedback available | Example task |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Supervised learning | Feature-outcome pairs $(X,Y)$ | Predict a 311 closure category or count |
| Unsupervised learning | Features $X$, with no specified outcome | Explore groups among requests with similar features |
| Reinforcement learning | States, actions, and rewards over time | Choose traffic-signal actions from traffic feedback |

: Common learning settings and the feedback they use. {#tbl-ml-settings}


Supervised learning uses examples with known outcomes to fit a rule that
predicts outcomes for new cases. Classification predicts a category, such as
whether a request closes within a stated time. Regression predicts a numeric
quantity, such as a count or duration. Logistic regression in @sec-modeling
is a classification method; the Poisson model is used there for a count
outcome.


Unsupervised learning looks for structure when the analysis has no specified
outcome to predict. Clustering assigns observations to groups based on their
features, and dimension reduction represents many features with fewer
quantities. These methods can help explore data, but a cluster is not
automatically a real-world kind of person or event. The result depends on
which observations and features are included, how they are measured, and how
the method is configured.


Reinforcement learning concerns a sequence of decisions. An agent observes a
state, chooses an action, and receives a reward after interacting with an
environment. The aim is to learn a policy, or rule for choosing actions, that
performs well over time. A reward is not simply a label attached to each
record: actions can change later states and rewards. This chapter introduces
the setting but does not develop reinforcement-learning algorithms
[@sutton2018reinforcement].


These three settings provide a useful introduction, but they do not cover
every learning design. For example, semi-supervised and self-supervised
methods use additional structures in the data. The right method depends on
the question, available feedback, and intended use of the result.


## Models and Algorithms

A model is a representation of a relationship or a rule for producing
predictions. A learning algorithm is the procedure that uses data to fit a
model. The distinction matters because different algorithms can fit models
for the same task, and a single algorithm can produce different fitted models
when its data or settings change.


Fitting a model estimates parameters from training data. In logistic
regression, the fitted coefficients are parameters. A hyperparameter controls
how the fitting procedure works rather than being estimated as an ordinary
model coefficient. The `C` setting in scikit-learn's regularized logistic
regression controls the strength of regularization; @sec-modeling tunes it
using cross-validation. A hyperparameter can change model complexity and
predictive performance [@scikitlearn2026logistic].


Statistical models remain central to machine learning. A generalized linear
model can estimate interpretable associations and make predictions. A more
flexible algorithm can capture patterns that a simple model misses, but its
predictions may be harder to explain and can be more sensitive to the
training data. The task determines which properties matter: predictive
accuracy, interpretability, uncertainty, computational cost, or a
combination of them.


## Generalization

A model is useful for prediction when it performs well on cases beyond those
used to fit it. This ability is called generalization. Training performance
describes how well a fitted model matches the data used for fitting; it does
not by itself measure performance on future or otherwise unseen cases.


Model complexity can create two different problems. An overly simple model
may miss structure in the data and perform poorly even on its training
observations. This is underfitting. A highly flexible model may match the
training observations closely, including chance variation that will not
repeat in new data. This is overfitting. Training error can keep decreasing
as flexibility increases, even while predictive error on new data increases.


The bias–variance tradeoff gives one account of why complexity affects
prediction. For a new numeric outcome independent of training data $D$,
suppose $Y=f(x)+\varepsilon$ at a fixed feature value $x$, where
$\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid x]=0$ and
$\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon\mid x)=\sigma^2$. If
$\widehat{f}_D(x)$ is a prediction from a model fitted to $D$, then its
expected squared prediction error can be decomposed as

$$
\mathbb{E}_{D,Y\mid x}\left[
  \{Y-\widehat{f}_D(x)\}^2
\right]
= \left\{\mathbb{E}_D[\widehat{f}_D(x)]-f(x)\right\}^2
+ \operatorname{Var}_D\left[\widehat{f}_D(x)\right]
+ \sigma^2,
$$

where the first term is squared bias, the second is variance across possible
training samples, and the final term is irreducible outcome variation under
these assumptions. A model with high bias tends to be too restrictive; a
model with high variance changes substantially when its training data
change. Greater flexibility can reduce bias while increasing variance, but
the balance depends on the data and the learning procedure. The decomposition
is a result for squared-error prediction under stated assumptions, not a
universal formula for every task. For classification and unsupervised
learning, the same words are sometimes used as intuition, but the
decomposition above does not directly apply [@james2023introduction].


## Evaluation and Tuning

Evaluation estimates how well a fitted model performs for the cases that
matter to its intended use. The data split should reflect that use. A random
split may be unsuitable when predictions concern future time periods,
unseen locations, or groups whose observations are dependent. In those
settings, a temporal or grouped split may give a more relevant assessment.


Training, validation, and test data serve different purposes. Training data
fit model parameters. Validation data compare candidate models or
hyperparameter settings. A test set is held aside for a final assessment
after the model and its settings have been selected. When data are limited,
cross-validation repeatedly divides the training data into fitting and
validation folds. Its score summarizes performance across those folds for a
chosen metric. The score depends on the split design and does not guarantee
performance under a different population or deployment setting
[@scikitlearn2026crossvalidation].


Tuning chooses hyperparameters, such as regularization strength or tree
depth. Clustering methods also have settings, such as the number of
clusters, that require criteria suited to an unsupervised task. The tuning
criterion should match the task and the costs of errors. In @sec-modeling,
cross-validation selects logistic regression's `C` by mean log loss, and an
untouched test set assesses the selected model. The chapter also explains
why using the same validation results both to select and report final
performance can make the reported score optimistic [@varma2006bias].


No single score answers every question. Accuracy summarizes the fraction of
correct classifications at a specified threshold, while log loss assesses
predicted probabilities and ROC AUC assesses ranking across thresholds.
Numeric outcomes require other measures, such as mean absolute error or
root mean squared error. The score should be interpreted with the baseline,
the prediction setting, and the consequences of errors in view
[@scikitlearn2026metrics]. The 311 example in @sec-modeling works through
these distinctions.


## Pipelines

A modeling pipeline connects data preparation steps to a final estimator.
For example, a classification pipeline may impute missing values, encode
categorical variables, scale numeric variables, and then fit a classifier.
The fitted pipeline applies the same sequence to new records when producing
predictions. In scikit-learn, a `Pipeline` or `make_pipeline` object
represents such a sequence; a `ColumnTransformer` can apply different
preparation steps to different columns [@scikitlearn2026composite].


Keeping preparation in the pipeline is essential during cross-validation.
Each fold must learn quantities such as scaling means, imputation values,
or category encodings from that fold's training records. It then applies
those learned transformations to the validation records. If the entire data
set determines a transformation before the split, information from
validation records can affect fitting and make the score too optimistic.
The example in @sec-modeling demonstrates a pipeline with mixed variable
types and shows how it works inside cross-validation.


A pipeline chains data transformations and a final estimator. Ensembles and
stacking combine predictions from multiple fitted models; they are different
algorithmic constructions. This chapter focuses on pipelines that combine
preprocessing steps with an estimator, as in @sec-modeling.


## Exercises {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ml-settings}
Classify each problem by its learning setting and identify the information
available to the learning procedure.

a. Predict whether a 311 request closes within one hour using labeled past
   requests. Identify the features and outcome.
b. Group requests by their recorded features without defining an outcome.
   State one reason the resulting groups may not represent real-world kinds
   of requests.
c. Choose traffic-signal actions over time and use later traffic flow as
   feedback. Identify the state, action, and reward.
d. For each problem, name one conclusion the fitted method alone cannot
   establish.
:::

::: {#exr-ml-generalization}
The table gives hypothetical training and cross-validation log losses for
three candidate models. Lower log loss indicates better probabilistic
predictions.

| Candidate | Training log loss | Mean cross-validation log loss |
|:--|--:|--:|
| A | 0.68 | 0.69 |
| B | 0.50 | 0.54 |
| C | 0.20 | 0.75 |

a. Which candidate appears to underfit? Explain using both scores.
b. Which candidate appears to overfit? Explain using the difference between
   its training and cross-validation scores.
c. Which candidate would you select based on these scores? State one reason
   the selected model's cross-validation score may not equal its future
   performance.
:::

::: {#exr-ml-pipeline}
Review a proposed workflow for tuning a classifier. The analyst first
standardizes numeric features using all observations, then creates
cross-validation folds and compares several values of the regularization
parameter.

a. Identify the source of information leakage in this workflow.
b. Describe how a pipeline would change the order of fitting and applying
   the standardization step.
c. Explain how the analyst should use a separate test set after selecting
   the regularization parameter.
d. State one reason a random cross-validation split may be unsuitable for
   data collected repeatedly over time.
:::
